extracted.intended_audience: college/university faculty and administrators (mathematics departments, curriculum committees) designing or evaluating undergraduate quantitative literacy/quantitative reasoning programs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and program-level criteria for creating, placing, assessing, and staffing an undergraduate Quantitative Literacy/Quantitative Reasoning requirement and its courses across the curriculum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student competency goals for revised mathematics foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: The student should be able to: understand and use numbers and mathematical symbols; think logically to solve problems; manipulate and understand algebraic expressions; model real life problems using mathematics; read and understand mathematical information in the media and professional literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the stated goals of the revised foundation requirement and may be demonstrated by placement examination or by completing with a passing grade college-level coursework equivalent to College Algebra, Mathematics for Elementary Teachers, Finite Mathematics, or Contemporary Mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course options aligned to intended audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide multiple course alternatives (e.g., College Algebra, Mathematics for the Elementary School Teacher, Finite Mathematics, Contemporary Mathematics) each targeted to clearly defined student audiences and major-specific needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each option should have an explicit intended audience (e.g., STEM majors needing algebra vs. prospective elementary teachers vs. service courses for business/computer science vs. general-interest students) so placement/advising can match students to the appropriate course and minimize later need for additional coursework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on applications and modeling across courses
rubrics_metrics.description: Courses (even those covering traditional topics) should emphasize applications and the modeling of real-life problems relevant to the student population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: use functions to discuss deforestation or cholesterol decline; introduce Newton's law of gravity when teaching variation; exponential functions for carbon-dating, half-lives, logistic growth models. For service courses, choose applied texts and examples in consultation with other departments (e.g., binary/hexadecimal for computer science).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary-teacher course: classroom relevance and manipulatives
rubrics_metrics.description: A course for prospective elementary teachers should stress relationship to elementary classroom content and use manipulatives as much as possible; content informed by state education standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include topics such as problem solving, sets, symbolic logic, numeration systems, geometry, and inductive/deductive reasoning; consider special materials (e.g., Fen Arithmetic) to help students experience arithmetic learning processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporary Mathematics course design flexibility with clear aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary Mathematics may have less well-defined curriculum; instructors choose overlapping topics with aims to demonstrate broad applications, engage students, and create informed users of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a list of possible topics (voting theory, graph theory, cryptography, statistics, etc.), limit coverage to a manageable number (typically five or six topics), and encourage projects/papers and student presentations when class size permits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class size and cap recommendations for active/problem-based courses
rubrics_metrics.description: Active/problem-working courses (e.g., Contemporary Mathematics) function best at small class sizes; optimal size no more than 15–18, and quality declines significantly above ~25.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Departmental caps should reflect pedagogical needs (e.g., cap Contemporary Mathematics at 25 though general caps may be 30) to allow in-class problem work, projects, and presentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement testing protocol and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a placement test plus secondary indicators (ACT math subscore, high-school math courses) to determine appropriate course placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example placement test: one hour, 36 multiple-choice questions covering material from basic skills through college algebra; use results in conjunction with other measures to assign to Basic Skills, Intermediate Algebra, one of the four college-algebra-equivalent options, combined precalculus/calculus, or Calculus I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advising procedures to ensure appropriate enrollments
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-part process: (1) placement testing; (2) advising component where advisors and students receive accurate, up-to-date information about placements and intended audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide written information to all advisors, have mathematics faculty attend advisor meetings, present to freshman advisors, make math faculty available during advising periods, visit intermediate algebra classes before advising, discuss placement options on first day of classes, and leverage word-of-mouth from satisfied students. Acknowledge limitations where meetings are not mandatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program assessment: course-level numeric and qualitative evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess courses numerically (e.g., SIR II forms) and qualitatively (common locally-created form) and also assess whether students are enrolled in the appropriate classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualitative forms should solicit written answers on organization, fairness, overall quality of teaching, stimulation of intellectual curiosity, and development of critical thinking. Use student satisfaction data and enrollment patterns (interpreted in institutional-growth context) to evaluate program success.

rubrics_metrics.name: QR Basic Skills requirement (Hollins): baseline competencies and assessment routes
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic skills requirement satisfied by passing a placement assessment or completing an introductory QR course; students who satisfy it will demonstrate baseline understanding of algebra, graphing, geometry, data analysis, and linearity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goals include understanding mathematical/statistical reasoning and using appropriate tools to summarize data, make predictions, and establish cause-and-effect. Incorporate hands-on labs (e.g., weekly Excel labs) teaching graphing, analysis, modeling growth, and financial topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: QR Applied Skills requirement: discipline-linked projects and outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Applied QR courses must give students the opportunity to apply quantitative skills in their chosen discipline and include at least two QR projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects should include data collection, discussion and collaborative analysis, use of appropriate technology, and culminate in a written assignment containing a statement of the problem, explanation of methods, summary of results, and when appropriate, limitations and possible improvements. Emphasize projects that advance course goals rather than rote procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty development as an implementation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Invest in faculty development (workshops, visiting scholars, cross-disciplinary discussion) to prepare instructors across disciplines to teach QR effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example activities: NSF-funded workshops, visiting scholars lecturing and leading workshops, multi-day faculty workshops to develop and critique QR projects; these activities foster cross-disciplinary connections and empower faculty to integrate QR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer and articulation policy considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for transfer students and state articulation agreements: community college general-education math courses may transfer in, but transferred courses cannot be guaranteed to meet local QR goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider requiring transfer students to take the placement test and meet with math-department advisors to determine placement; develop procedures for students who place below the level of a course for which they already have credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evening/part-time student access and course offering constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that limited evening offerings constrain part-time students' options and that adjunct staffing may limit which QR options can be offered in the evening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where demand and instructor availability justify it, consider adding evening sections (e.g., Contemporary Mathematics) and ensure appropriate instructors (preferably full-time faculty) are available to teach them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use enrollment trends and qualitative feedback to judge program success
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitor enrollments by course option over time and combine quantitative trends with qualitative student feedback to evaluate whether program goals (e.g., increased student interest, reduced anxiety about mathematics, appropriate placements) are being met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret enrollment shifts in context (e.g., institutional growth) and use student comments/surveys to assess satisfaction and learning outcomes; e.g., high satisfaction in Contemporary Mathematics indicated by qualitative student comments.
